children: By Alison Sider

For hours, Southwest Airlines Chief Operating Officer Andrew Watterson was hunkered in a situation room at the carrier's Dallas headquarters, trying to avoid gridlock at airports and to figure out how to prevent the Federal Aviation Administration's ground stop Friday from spiraling into an operational meltdown.

A pressing issue: finding places for the mounting numbers of planes on airport tarmacs to park. Airports were warning they were running out of concrete. Inside the situation room, everyone knew they had to unload planes and move them away from gates as quickly as possible to avoid backups that would have left passengers sitting for hours on tarmacs.

Soon after the ground stop was issued, the airline sent emails and other messages to gate agents ordering baggage checking to halt. Luggage could easily end up being stranded as flights got held and reshuffled.
Stopping all departing aircraft around the country is "extraordinarily, extraordinarily rare," said Watterson. "A couple times in one's career, at most."

On his iPad in the situation room, Watterson watched video calls that FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford held to update industry leaders, sometimes turning the volume up so deputies next to him could hear.

Periodically, Watterson and other leaders dashed out to the control center next door, where the carrier oversees thousands of daily flights and tens of thousands of pilots and flight attendants. There, the executives conferred with the crew schedulers and dispatchers who were dealing with the aftereffects of the ground stop on planes and crews.

Southwest officials gamed out different outcomes depending on when the FAA lifted the ground stop. At one point, it seemed like the airline might pull the plug on the rest of the evening, said Capt. Jody Reven, who heads the union that represents Southwest pilots. Some other airlines did.

Then Reven got a text from a Southwest executive in the situation room with the news. "'Hey, man we may be able to move some metal in like 20 minutes," the message said. He shared the news with union representatives in crew bases who field calls with questions from pilots. Planes were allowed to resume takeoffs about 8:15 p.m. ET. The airline had learned through painful experiences how quickly decisions need to be made at the start of a crisis. Its own sluggish decision-making, Southwest concluded, was a key factor in its meltdown following winter storm Elliott over Christmas in 2022 that forced the airline to cancel close to 17,000 flights and stranded passengers, bags and crews across the country.

To avoid the pitfalls that had paralyzed its operations during that disruption, the airline developed plans for different scenarios. It regularly held mock exercises. Just a week earlier, its on-call support team had drilled the scramble for hotel rooms during disruptions.

After the FAA issued the ground stop, Watterson, a former Army signals-intelligence analyst who has worked 13 years at Southwest, and his team had to put into action what was now the first step of a well-rehearsed playbook: act quickly.
Once flights resumed, Southwest implemented the rest of the playbook: avoid mass cancellations and get planes, pilots and flight attendants moving again.

The airline needed to get as many of them to their scheduled destination as possible, even though they had already missed flights. If they couldn't get to where they needed to be for the beginning of the day Saturday, the whole weekend could unravel.
Southwest planes generally hopscotch the country from one city to the next, rather than orbit a massive hub. So a disruption early in the chain can have knock-on effects.

Pilots and flight attendants needed hotel rooms to get the requisite rest to be able to legally fly again. With every airline — and stranded passengers — trying to solve the same problem, there was a severe hotel-room crunch.

The airline and the union told pilots that they could book their own hotels and get reimbursed, Reven said. It learned from the winter storm Elliott meltdown to not penny pinch on reservations and recovery efforts, the union chief said, and offered as much as double-pay to encourage pilots and flight attendants to pick up extra flights.

Southwest flew 150 crew members from Denver to Phoenix because there were no available hotel rooms. Even Phoenix didn't have enough: Some crew members had to stay in Sedona, Ariz., and make the two-hour drive to Phoenix the next morning. Some flight attendants lucked out and got rooms at the Four Seasons Hotel Las Vegas.
Southwest booked rooms even if it wasn't sure crews would need them. "I was, like, I'm buying insurance," Watterson said. "So we grabbed as many as we could."
Analysts estimate the ground stop cost Southwest as much as $135 million, partly because of labor and other expenses.
By 11 p.m. Friday in Dallas, Watterson said, he breathed a sigh of relief. He knew the airline would be able to operate Saturday, though with a lot of disruption.

There was still a lot of work ahead. About 400 planes had been slated to get inspected overnight Friday to be able to fly the next day. That meant making sure that the planes flew to cities with maintenance facilities, or that a mechanic or contractor would be available to meet the plane.

Dispatchers and crew schedulers worked until 3 a.m. Saturday morning going through the airline's sequences of flights for each plane, creating new trips for pilots and flight attendants to pick up. Some 2,400 flights didn't have the crew they needed. By the end of the day Saturday, 500 uncrewed flights remained. By Sunday morning, things were almost back to normal.

Over the course of the weekend, Southwest added about 300 extra flights to get everything back in place. Some were for passengers. In other cases, when it couldn't get a full complement of staff to be able to carry passengers, planes flew with only pilots and flight attendants aboard to help get the airline's schedule back to normal. Southwest canceled more than 2,000 or about 18% of its flights from Friday through Sunday — a smaller share than almost all of its rivals.
